extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, evolutionary biologists, and educated readers studying sexual selection and ornamentation
extracted.subtask_short: explaining bird ornaments by sexual selection
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of how complex plumage ornaments (ocelli, zoned feathers, elongated tail-coverts, etc.) can arise by small, successive changes and be fixed by sexual selection, using comparative anatomy, variation within individuals, and examples from related species. Emphasises gradation, correlation, and pigment-redistribution mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation of secondary characters between sexes and across body regions
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in one character (e.g., hackle-shaped feathers on the male's head) are often correlated with changes in other characters (e.g., colours of neck and loins), so that modifications tend to co-occur across parts of the body or between sexes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in certain breeds (golden and silver-spangled Polish, Houdans, Creve-coeur) hackles on the male's head correlate with hackles on neck and loins; the same correlation appears in natural species such as Gold and Amherst pheasants. Correlation explains why breeders can rear symmetric plumage patterns and why multiple parts of a male become ornamented together under selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feather structure yields symmetrical colouring
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure of each individual feather generally causes any change in its colouring to be symmetrical; consequently, feathers produce symmetrically shaded patterns across the plumage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed in laced, spangled, and pencilled breeds of fowl; shafts and barbule arrangement can determine tint distribution (examples of mongrel fowls with symmetric curved zones on each feather). This structural constraint allows selection to produce symmetric, species-like patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention of conserved marks despite overall colour change
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when overall plumage colour changes among species or breeds, certain spots, marks, or stripes are commonly retained across all forms (e.g., two wing-bars in pigeons), sometimes even inverted in colour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: pigeons retain two wing-bars though coloured variously; an aboriginal pigeon with blue tail has sub-varieties with white tail but the same pattern element inverted in colour. Such conserved elements can serve as scaffolds for further ornament evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and elementary nature of an ocellus
rubrics_metrics.description: An ocellus consists of a spot within a ring of another colour, often with additional concentric zones; the central spot may be surrounded by successive coloured zones producing the eye-like appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiar examples include peacock tail-coverts and the peacock-butterfly. Because ocelli are highly variable in some groups (e.g., Lepidoptera), their formation is likely to be a comparatively simple developmental/variationary process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ocellus formation by contraction/breaking up of stripes or blotches
rubrics_metrics.description: Circular spots (ocelli) are often generated by the breaking up and contraction of stripes or blotches of colour; a dark spot can be formed by pigment drawn centripetally, while a white spot can arise by pigment being driven away from a centre so that it accumulates in a surrounding zone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: gradations in butterflies (Hipparchia janira, Cyllo leda) from blotches or minute dots into perfect ocelli; guinea-fowl feathers with white spots and dark surrounding zones. This mechanism explains simple ocellus formation without invoking complex novelties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pigment redistribution (nearly constant quantity moved centripetally or centrifugally)
rubrics_metrics.description: The colouring matter seems to be a nearly constant quantity, but is redistributed either centripetally (toward a centre, producing a dark spot) or centrifugally (away from a centre, producing a white spot surrounded by darker zone).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains formation of ocelli and zoned feathers by redistribution of existing pigment rather than large changes in pigment amount. Examples include guinea-fowl and Argus plumage patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradation principle: complexity via small successive steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Highly complex ornaments may be acquired by small successive steps; presence of intermediate forms (either among related species or among feathers on the same individual) demonstrates plausible gradual pathways of development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach: compare many species of a group or examine different feathers on the same bird to trace successive modifications. The peacock and Polyplectron species provide a clear graded series from simple spots to elaborate ocelli and elongated tail-coverts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of comparative series (related species) to infer intermediate steps
rubrics_metrics.description: To discover the steps by which an ornament arose, compare all species of a large group; some species will retain traces of former characters and provide clues to intermediate states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Polyplectron species show intermediate characters (ocellated tail-coverts, partial confluence of ocelli, lengthened tail-coverts) that approach the peacock's condition; analysis of relative positions and degrees of confluence (e.g., two ocelli becoming confluent leaving indentations) elucidates transitional morphology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Within-individual gradation (feather-to-feather series) as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Different feathers on the same bird often present an almost continuous gradation from simple spots to perfect ocelli (or from basal spots to elliptic ornaments to ball-and-socket ocelli), demonstrating feasible small steps toward complex ornaments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argus pheasant secondary wing-feathers: basal feathers show only larger basal spots; slightly more distal feathers show elliptic ornaments composed of several marks and shaded zones; still further feathers show intermediate ocelli and finally perfect ball-and-socket ocelli (with ring and shaded ball). This feather-series provides a direct demonstration of stepwise development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of ring structures from convergence and confluence of multiple marks
rubrics_metrics.description: The black ring surrounding an ocellus is formed by the union and modification of several elongated black marks which become confluent and more circular by successive changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Argus feathers, three marks (labelled b, c, d) unite and modify to form the ring; traces of junctions and indentations in perfect ocelli often reveal this origin. Thus detailed micro-patterns (breaks, thickenings) are signatures of their composite origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Development of shading to produce three-dimensional (ball-and-socket) effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The three-dimensional, ball-like appearance of certain ocelli is produced by precise shading: a thickened and interrupted ring, an oblique bright (white) mark representing reflected light, and graduated shading from pale to dark across the enclosed 'ball'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: the ring is often broken at a point above the white shade; the lower part of the ball is browner and the upper part paler, producing convex shading. Gradual enhancement of the elliptic ornament's internal shading yields the ball-and-socket effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of imperfect structures as transitional evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Imperfect or atypical features (e.g., ocelli lacking the upper thickened part, ocelli with indentations) are interpreted as intermediate or derivative states, not as flaws to invalidate gradual evolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: uppermost ocelli on some feathers appear 'sliced off' where stripes are abruptly cut; indentations in peacock ocelli indicate double origin from confluence. Imperfections are expected because selection for ornament need not produce absolute perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female preference as causal agent of ornament elaboration (sexual selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Continued preference by females for the most beautiful males will unconsciously increase the attractiveness of males over generations, resulting in exaggerated ornamentation (sexual selection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and evidence: peacock train likely developed because females preferred more beautiful males; observed courtship displays in humming-birds and reports that ornament and variety are the 'sole object' in some genera. Sexual selection is posited as the most plausible explanation when natural selection cannot account for specific ornamental varieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domesticated variation and immature plumage as analogues for evolutionary steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes observed in domesticated birds and in the immature plumage of young birds can indicate probable steps by which wild males acquired brilliant plumage and ornaments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin references extraordinary variability in domesticated breeds and characteristics of immature plumage as supporting evidence that small, graded changes sufficed to build complex ornaments.

rubrics_metrics.name: High instability/variability of marking characters facilitates evolution of ocelli
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters of mere marking or coloration (especially in Lepidoptera) are very unstable in number and size, enabling rapid and diverse modifications such as the development or loss of ocelli.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr. Trimen's and Mr. Wallace's observations of great variation in butterfly ocelli (e.g., Cyllo leda, Hipparchia janira) provide direct evidence that complex patterns can arise relatively easily from variable markings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of ornament shading with display posture and illumination
rubrics_metrics.description: The placement of highlights and shading in ocelli often aligns with the way the bird displays its feathers and the typical direction of illumination, so that ocelli on differently oriented feathers appear as if illuminated from above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in the peacock the white marks representing reflected light are placed so that feathers held vertically or horizontally both appear lit from above; slight systematic deviations (white marks a bit too far toward the further end) indicate imperfect but directionally consistent adaptation for visual effect during display.
